description: Smuggling, highwaymen, Luddites, Jack the Ripper, car crime, terrorism and cybercrime.
content_html:
New Crimes in the Eighteenth Century

By the eighteenth century, the nature of crime in Britain was changing in response to new economic conditions. Two crimes in particular captured the public imagination: smuggling and highway robbery. Both thrived because of gaps in the state’s ability to police a large, sparsely supervised country, and both acquired a romantic popular reputation that distorted how they were actually experienced by victims.

Smuggling became a major organised activity along the south and east coasts of England. High customs duties on tea, brandy, tobacco and silk — imposed partly to fund expensive wars — made illegal importation enormously profitable. Gangs such as the Hawkhurst Gang in Kent and Sussex operated openly in the 1740s and 1750s, sometimes numbering in the hundreds and terrifying communities into silence. Smuggling was not seen as a serious moral crime by many local people who benefited from cheap smuggled goods; this popular sympathy made it very hard to police.

Key Fact

Smuggling flourished in the eighteenth century because high customs duties made it hugely profitable, policing was thin along the coastline, and local communities often sympathised with or participated in the trade. Organised gangs such as the Hawkhurst Gang operated on a significant scale in the 1740s and 1750s.

Highway Robbery

Highway robbery was facilitated by the growth of coach travel and the movement of goods between expanding towns and cities. Highwaymen preyed on travellers and coaches carrying valuables. Figures such as Dick Turpin — a real criminal executed at York in 1739, though far more brutal in reality than his romanticised legend — became popular folk heroes. The actual experience of highway robbery was violent and terrifying; the myth of the “gentlemanly highwayman” was largely a literary invention. By the late eighteenth century, improved roads, better banking and organised thief-taking had reduced highwaymen significantly.

Industrial and Agrarian Disorder

Industrialisation generated entirely new categories of collective crime — criminal by law, but understood by participants as protest. The Luddites were skilled textile workers in the Midlands and North who smashed the frames and machinery that were replacing them in 1811–1813. The government treated the movement as insurrection: the Frame Breaking Act of 1812 made machine-breaking a capital offence, and troops were deployed in larger numbers than Wellington then had in the Peninsular War. By 1813, the movement had collapsed under military and judicial repression.

Agricultural labourers in the south of England staged a similar protest in 1830. The Swing Riots took their name from the fictional “Captain Swing” — a threatening letter signed by this name was sent to landlords across the southern counties demanding higher wages and the withdrawal of threshing machines. Around 1,500 incidents of arson and machine-breaking were recorded. The government’s response was severe: 19 rioters were executed and around 500 transported to Australia.

Victorian cities generated new forms of crime suited to their conditions. Overcrowded slums in London, Manchester and Birmingham hosted gangs of pick-pockets, prostitution networks and receivers of stolen goods (“fences”). The Jack the Ripper murders of 1888, in which five women were killed in the East End of London, highlighted the extreme poverty of urban slum life and the limitations of the Metropolitan Police’s detective capacity. The case was never solved and became a landmark in the public understanding of urban crime.

Key Fact

The Swing Riots of 1830 involved agricultural labourers destroying threshing machines across southern England. The government executed 19 rioters and transported approximately 500 to Australia. The protests reflected desperation over low wages and mechanisation — but the law treated them as straightforward criminal disorder.

The twentieth century introduced a proliferation of new crime categories, most of them tied to new technologies or social changes. The spread of the motor car created offences such as speeding, drink-driving, driving without insurance and vehicle theft. By the late twentieth century, car crime was among the most commonly recorded crime categories in England and Wales. Football hooliganism emerged from the 1960s onwards, linked to gang culture, alcohol and urban deindustrialisation. The government responded with legislation including the Football (Offences) Act 1991 and banning orders.

Terrorism became a defining crime of the later twentieth century. The Provisional IRA conducted a sustained bombing campaign in Britain from the 1970s, including the Birmingham pub bombings of 1974 and the Brighton hotel bombing of 1984. Islamist terrorism became the dominant concern after the 9/11 attacks of 2001; the 7 July 2005 bombings in London killed 52 people and reshaped counter-terrorism policy. The internet enabled cybercrime on a scale previously impossible — organised fraud, ransomware attacks, identity theft and the online distribution of illegal material became major challenges for law enforcement by the 2000s and 2010s.
exam_tip_html: The 16-mark thematic change essay is likely to ask how far the nature of crime changed across all three eras. To reach the top band, cover the medieval era (petty theft, violence), the early modern era (vagrancy, heresy, collective protest), and the modern era (car crime, terrorism, cybercrime). A common mistake is treating the nineteenth century as ‘modern’ — examiners want you to reach the twentieth or twenty-first century for full credit. Show continuity too: poverty-driven crime and property crime persist in every era even as new categories emerge.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Smuggling and highway robbery dominated eighteenth-century crime, both driven by economic opportunity and weak policing; the Hawkhurst Gang and Dick Turpin became notorious symbols of the era.
  • Industrial unrest produced new collective crimes: the Luddites (1811-1813) smashed machinery; the Swing Riots (1830) saw agricultural workers protest against mechanisation — both suppressed by severe state force.
  • The twentieth century introduced entirely new crime types: motor vehicle offences, football hooliganism, terrorism (IRA; Islamist) and cybercrime — each a product of new technologies and social conditions.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of smuggling as a crime in eighteenth-century Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Feature may include: high customs duties made it profitable; organised gangs (e.g. Hawkhurst Gang) operated openly; local communities sympathised and participated; coastline was difficult to police. Simple identification (1 mark); developed with specific detail (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Luddite movement (1811-1813).
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: Luddites were skilled framework knitters and textile workers who smashed industrial machinery threatening their livelihoods; the movement was concentrated in the Midlands and North of England. Feature 2: The government responded with extreme severity — the Frame Breaking Act of 1812 made machine-breaking a capital offence and troops were deployed in greater numbers than Wellington had in the Peninsular War at the time.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why new types of crime emerged in the twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names a new crime category. Developing: Links it to a new technology or social change. Secure: Explains how the motor car created entirely new crime categories impossible before its invention; uses specific examples (drink-driving, vehicle theft); notes the volume of new offences it generated. Mastering: Sustains analysis of how technological change (motor car, internet) consistently generates new crime categories; may compare with how eighteenth-century trade routes generated smuggling and highwaymen in the same way — technology creating both opportunity and crime.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Swing Riots of 1830 as evidence about crime and punishment in early nineteenth-century Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Describes what happened. Developing: Notes government used severe punishment. Secure: Analyses significance at the time: the government's use of execution and transportation showed that it treated collective protest as a threat to social order; the riots revealed the gap between legal definitions of crime and popular views of justice. Mastering: Evaluates significance over time: the Swing Riots represent a pattern of criminalising collective protest that continued into the nineteenth century (trade union activity was criminalised by the Combination Acts); they also demonstrate continuity with earlier agrarian disorder driven by poverty.

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that the nature of crime in Britain changed significantly between the eighteenth and twenty-first centuries?
Give reasons for your answer and refer to different periods in your response.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments for significant change: entirely new categories emerged (car crime, cybercrime, terrorism); organised crime became more sophisticated; the scale of fraud expanded with the internet; terrorism by non-state actors is a modern phenomenon. Arguments for continuity: property crime and theft have remained dominant throughout; violence has always been present; collective protest crime (Luddites-to-miners' strike) shows a recurring pattern. Emerging: one-sided or superficial. Developing: notes changes but without sustained argument. Secure: argues a clear position with evidence from at least two periods. Mastering: evaluates the degree of change against continuity, uses specific evidence from multiple periods, reaches a justified overall conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of terrorism as a crime in the late twentieth century in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: The Provisional IRA conducted a sustained bombing campaign in Britain from the 1970s; major attacks included the Birmingham pub bombings (1974) and Brighton hotel bombing (1984). Feature 2: Islamist terrorism became the dominant concern after 2001; the 7 July 2005 bombings in London killed 52 people and reshaped counter-terrorism legislation and policing priorities.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did smuggling become a major organised crime in eighteenth-century England?
flashcard_questions.a: High customs duties on tea, brandy and tobacco made illegal importation enormously profitable.

flashcard_questions.q: The Hawkhurst Gang was involved in what crime and in which decade did they operate?
flashcard_questions.a: Smuggling, operating in Kent and Sussex in the 1740s and 1750s.
Robbery committed on public roads by mounted criminals, a major problem in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

flashcard_questions.q: Dick Turpin was executed in what year and where?
Who were the Luddites and what did they do?
flashcard_questions.a: Skilled textile workers who smashed industrial machinery threatening their livelihoods, 1811-1813.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the government's legislative response to the Luddite movement?
flashcard_questions.a: The Frame Breaking Act of 1812 made machine-breaking a capital offence.

flashcard_questions.q: What were the Swing Riots of 1830?
flashcard_questions.a: Agricultural labourers in southern England destroying threshing machines and sending threatening letters to landlords.

flashcard_questions.q: How many Swing Rioters were executed by the government?

flashcard_questions.a: Disorder and violence by football supporters, associated with organised gang clashes, prominent in Britain from the 1960s to the 1990s.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one major IRA bombing attack in mainland Britain.
flashcard_questions.a: The Birmingham pub bombings of 1974 (also valid: Brighton hotel bombing, 1984).

flashcard_questions.q: When did the 7 July London bombings occur and how many people were killed?
Give one example of a crime type created by the internet in the late twentieth century.
flashcard_questions.a: Cybercrime — for example, online fraud, ransomware attacks or identity theft.

glossary_terms.definition: The illegal importation of goods (particularly spirits, tea and tobacco) to avoid paying customs duties, widespread in eighteenth-century Britain.
Robbery committed on public roads by mounted criminals, a major problem on English roads in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
Framework knitters and textile workers who destroyed industrial machinery between 1811 and 1813, protesting against mechanisation that threatened their livelihoods.
A wave of agricultural unrest in 1830, in which labourers destroyed threshing machines and sent threatening 'Captain Swing' letters to landlords to protest against low wages and mechanisation.
Disorder and violence by football supporters, especially associated with organised gang clashes at or around matches, prominent in Britain from the 1960s to the 1990s.
Criminal activity carried out using computers or the internet, such as fraud, hacking, ransomware or identity theft.
